corrected_value.title: Comparing the effects of derived relational training and computer coding on intellectual potential in school-age children.

decision.location: Discussion, page 21; Introduction, pages 11-13; References, page 34
decision.quote:
Previous analyses have reported increases in verbal intelligence following relational 

skills training interventions, a finding which is replicated in the current analysis (Cassidy et 

al., 2011; 2016; Hayes & Stewart, 2016). The Verbal IQ rises reported in the current study 

(M=19.6 points) are similar to the 18 point increase reported in Cassidy et al. (2011) which 

used a small sample of 8- to 12-year old children. Hayes and Stewart (2016) also report 

significant rises in a number of verbal indices, such as WIAT Spelling, WIAT Reading, 

WISC Letter Number Sequencing and WISC Digit Span following SMART training, 

indicating that improvements in IQ scores following SMART training may further extend to 

increments in scholastic aptitude.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: in 'The Current Study' (pp. 12-13), the authors state that prior SMART studies (including Hayes & Stewart, 2016) used non-blinded testers, and administer the relational skills training intervention used by Hayes & Stewart (2016) with WASI pre/post testing (which Hayes & Stewart, 2016 also used, finding significant WASI Block Design and verbal index improvements, p. 11) in a single-blind RCT to interrogate the reported effects. In the Discussion (pp. 21, 24-25), the authors explicitly state that the increase in verbal intelligence following relational skills training in Hayes & Stewart (2016) is replicated in the current analysis and compare their effects to Hayes & Stewart's (2016) active-control findings. (2) Identity: cited in text and listed in References (p. 34) as Hayes, J. & Stewart, I. (2016), 'Comparing the effects of derived relational training and computer coding on intellectual potential in school-age children', British Journal of Educational Psychology, 86, 397-411, DOI 10.1111/bjep.12114 (verified in Crossref metadata). (3) Absence and non-equivalence: absent from shipped row input_row_index 20 (Cassidy et al., 2016, DOI 10.1016/j.lindif.2016.03.001) and distinct from sibling targets 0, 3, and 4, as Hayes & Stewart (2016) is an independent study of 28 children aged 10-11 comparing SMART training against Scratch computer coding.

corrected_value.title: Assessing the Effects of a Relational Training Intervention on Fluid Intelligence Among a Sample of Socially Disadvantaged Children in Bangladesh.

decision.location: Discussion, page 26; Introduction, pages 12-13; References, page 28
decision.quote:
However, a post-hoc 

analysis found that the collective Full Scale IQ gain found for participants who failed to 

complete the training program was 18.2 points, an average increase only marginally lower 

than that found for those who completed all 55 levels (M = 19.1 points).  As such, the 

number of training levels completed was not a predictor of subsequent IQ gains (as 

confirmed by correlational analyses), which is inconsistent with the “dosage effects” reported 

in the Amd & Roche (in press) study.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: the authors describe Amd & Roche (in press) as finding significant IQ gains after SMART training that were not accounted for by baseline IQ and a significant positive correlation between training progress and IQ gain (p. 12). In 'The Current Study' (pp. 12-13), they cite the absence of a control group and non-blinded testing in Amd & Roche (in press) as requiring an improved single-blind RCT replication administering the SMART intervention used by Amd & Roche (in press). In Results (p. 17) and Discussion (pp. 24, 26), the authors test both IQ gains (and their independence from baseline IQ) and whether the number of completed training levels predicts IQ gains, explicitly contrasting their null correlation within the trained group with the 'dosage effects' reported by Amd & Roche (in press). (2) Identity: cited in text and listed in References (p. 28) as Amd, M. & Roche, B. (in press), 'Assessing the Effects of a Relational Training Intervention on Fluid Intelligence Among a Sample of Socially Disadvantaged Children in Bangladesh', The Psychological Record (no DOI printed). (3) Absence and non-equivalence: completely distinct from shipped row input_row_index 20 (Cassidy et al., 2016, Irish schoolchildren) and from sibling targets 0, 2, and 4, as it reports an independent study of socially disadvantaged children in Bangladesh.

corrected_value.authors: Thirus, J., Starbrink, M. & Jansson, B.
corrected_value.title: Relational frame theory, mathematical and logical skills: A multiple exemplar training intervention to enhance intellectual performance.

decision.location: Introduction, pages 11-13; Results, page 20; References, page 42
decision.quote:
The current study is the first to implement blind testing in the study of relational skills 

training programs in a randomized controlled trial of the SMART method. Thus, it does not 

aim to replicate previous studies precisely but aims to interrogate the reported effects using 

more stringent methodologies. Indeed, this is the optimal way in which to test the theoretical 

hypotheses underlying an intervention rather than the methodologies per se (see Crandall & 

Sherman, 2016 for a more complete discussion of the relative merits of direct and conceptual 

replication).  In this study, the relational skills training intervention used by Amd and Roche 

(in press), Cassidy et al. (2016), Hayes and Stewart (2016), and Thirus et al. (2016) was 

administered to a group of 15 to 17-year-old children over a period of three months using a 

single-blind randomized controlled design. Scores on a standardized assessment of 

intelligence (Wechsler Abbreviated Scale of Intelligence, WASi, Wechsler, 1999) were 

administered to all participants before and after completing the training program, in order to 

assess its impact on intellectual performance.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. (1) Empirical retesting: the paper summarizes Thirus et al. (2016) as a controlled study of 21 high school students aged 16-18 years showing significantly greater increases in intellectual performance on Raven's Standard Progressive Matrices following 8-10 weeks of SMART training (pp. 11-12). In 'The Current Study' (pp. 12-13), the authors critique the non-blinded testing across the published SMART studies and explicitly design their single-blind RCT in 15- to 17-year-old secondary students using the SMART intervention from Amd & Roche (in press), Cassidy et al. (2016), Hayes & Stewart (2016), and Thirus et al. (2016) to interrogate the reported intellectual-performance effects (including WASI Full Scale IQ, Performance IQ, and Matrix Reasoning, p. 20). (2) Identity: cited in text and listed in References (p. 42) as Thirus, J., Starbrink, M. & Jansson, B. (2016), 'Relational frame theory, mathematical and logical skills: A multiple exemplar training intervention to enhance intellectual performance', International Journal of Psychology & Psychological Therapy, 16(2), 141-155 (no DOI printed). (3) Absence and non-equivalence: absent from shipped row input_row_index 20 (Cassidy et al., 2016, Learning and Individual Differences) and distinct from sibling targets 0, 2, and 3.
